title: Philippi
lead: A city in eastern Macedonia, refounded as a Roman colony after the battle of Philippi in 42 BC. Paul founded his first church in Europe there, with Lydia and the jailer among its first believers, and later wrote it the Letter to the Philippians.

sections.b: Settlers from Thasos founded Crenides in 360/359 BC; Philip II of Macedon took it in 356 BC and gave it his name. After Mark Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius on the plain west of the city in October 42 BC, Philippi was refounded as a Roman colony and veterans were settled there; after 27 BC it was Colonia Augusta Iulia Philippensis. Its many Latin inscriptions show a 'miniature Rome' on the route of the Via Egnatia. Its ruins, near Kavala in Greece, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.

Acts tells how Paul and his companions came to Philippi, likely about AD 49 or 50: Lydia and the women at the place of prayer, the slave girl with a Python spirit, the beating, the earthquake and the jailer's household, and Paul's claim to be a Roman citizen (Acts 16:12-40). The church later supported Paul more than once (Philippians 4:15-16; 2 Corinthians 11:9), and Paul passed through again (Acts 20:1-6).

In a city proud of its Roman status, Paul tells the church to 'live as citizens worthy of the good news of Christ' (Philippians 1:27) and says 'we belong to a commonwealth in heaven' (Philippians 3:20). The verb and the noun he uses, politeuomai and politeuma, appear nowhere else in his letters.
